activities.caption: pair each film with its colour system
activities.name: mesColourMatch

config.prompt: Three colour systems, three jobs — pair them:

pairs.right: a character's signature — the resurrection recognised before the plot admits it
a temperature choice — candlelit interiors while the family negotiates murder
one painting per sequence — the palette arcs with the story before shots exist

config.why: In analysis, list a frame's two or three dominant colours and ask what they attach to — recurring pairings are the film's rhyme scheme.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the lighting lecture
activities.name: mesLightSpot

config.prompt: A lighting lecture contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Three-point lighting — key, fill, backlight — is the default grammar.
Kubrick bought NASA-spec Zeiss lenses rated at f/0.7 so Barry Lyndon's interiors could be lit by actual candles.
Gordon Willis lit The Godfather brightly and evenly, so Brando's eyes would always read clearly.
The mechanism is constant: light directs attention and assigns moral register.
A face half in shadow is a thesis about that character.
config.correction: Willis's golden top-light left Brando's eyes black pits — deliberate underexposure, darkness as moral climate.
config.why: Hard light interrogates; soft light forgives — the argument lives in the deviation from the default grammar.

activities.anchor: Willis's negatives were controlled to the stop
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the too-dark dailies
activities.name: mesDarkPredict

config.q: Studio executives complained that The Godfather's footage looked too dark. What happened?
choices: The film was brightened before release
The filmmakers were overruled on the complaint — and the style won history
config.why: The negatives were controlled to the stop — the darkness was the moral climate, not sloppiness. (The Oscar went elsewhere; the style won history.)

activities.anchor: constructs relations the stage never had
activities.caption: file each case: the join as argument, or the join as invisible
activities.name: mesCutBuckets

config.prompt: Two editing traditions — file each case:

items.label: Kuleshov's workshop: one neutral face, a bowl of soup, a coffin
2001's match cut from bone to orbiting weapon

config.why: Both traditions are worth reading: one writes history with the join, the other hides it so the story flows.

activities.anchor: is editing's negation and mise-en-scène's showcase
activities.caption: the cut versus the long take — drag between them
activities.name: mesTakeCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to hold a scene — drag the divider:

before.label: the cut
before.text: Editing's timescale trick: Kane's breakfast-table montage folds two decades of a marriage into a couple of minutes, each iteration one degree colder.

after.label: the long take
after.text: Rope pretends to be one continuous shot, forcing the thriller to be staged in real time across a moving camera; Children of Men traps the viewer inside the space exactly as the protagonist is.

config.why: An unbroken interval concentrates blocking, light, depth and performance into one shot — that is why a great long take feels like theatre caught alive.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the three-way sound taxonomy
activities.name: mesSoundCloze

config.text: Sound's taxonomy is three-way: %%0%% sound lives inside the story world; %%1%% sound — score and narration — is addressed to us; and in Jaws, John Williams's %%2%% figure substitutes for the star, putting the shark in the audience's nervous system so the film can show it rarely.
config.hint: A song on a radio that swells into the score lives on the border between the two.

activities.caption: Brando versus Ozu — drag between the schools
activities.name: mesActCompare

config.prompt: Two disciplined systems of performance — drag the divider:

before.label: Brando's Vito Corleone
before.text: Character built from physical business — the padded jaw, the stray cat found on the set, the hands doing the talking while the face does the hiding.

after.label: Ozu's players
after.text: Underplay almost to stillness — the emotion lands because the frame refuses it.

config.why: Both are disciplined systems; neither is 'natural.' The useful question is what behaviour was chosen, and what the staging does with it.

activities.anchor: The method that produces essayable results
activities.caption: rebuild the five-pass method
activities.name: mesPassOrder

config.prompt: One scene, five passes — put the method in order:
items: Watch muted — do the power relations survive?
Inventory a single frame — setting, light, colour, blocking, eyelines
Map the blocking — who moves, who is still, who owns the depth
Listen with eyes shut — what does the soundtrack stage?
Ask the cut — why does this shot end now?
config.why: Then compare stagings across the film: the same room shot twice with changed geometry is the form's return-with-change, spatialised.
